deep.reconstruction:
This page sets up Euler's constitutive law for wall friction in pipe flow (E260, 1761).

Setup: a tube ABCD carries water. Take a slice MNmn with axial length ds, wetted perimeter u and cross-sectional area zz. The wall pressure in the slice is expressed as a hydrostatic head p, the depth at which a wall immersed in still water would feel the same pressure. The lateral wall surface of the slice is u ds, so the normal force on it equals the weight of a water volume p u ds.

Friction law (sec. 9): by analogy with Coulomb/Amontons dry friction for solids (sec. 6-7 on the previous page), the friction force is a fixed fraction of the normal force: F = λ p u ds, with λ small and to be found by experiment. The slice's mass (in weight units) is zz ds. The retarding acceleration, in units of g, is therefore λ p u/zz.

Geometry (sec. 10): the retardation depends on the shape of the section only through the ratio u/zz, i.e. perimeter over area, the reciprocal of the modern hydraulic radius.
- Rectangle m by n: u = 2(m+n), zz = mn, so retardation = 2λp(m+n)/(mn).
- Square (m = n): retardation = 4λp/n.
- Circle: Euler writes u = 2πn and zz = πn², giving 2λp/n.

Sec. 11 (continued on the next page): with n = z/√π the circular retardation becomes 2λp√π/z. Euler absorbs the constant into α, so retardation = αp/z with λ = α/(2√π).

Purpose: this gives the friction term for the steady-flow equations for a vessel draining through a variable pipe, worked out on the following pages. Because friction depends on pressure and pressure depends on velocity, the problem must be solved simultaneously (sec. 12).
errors: Sec. 10 says the circle has 'diametrum ... = n', but the formulas u = 2πn and zz = πnn are those for radius n. With a true diameter n one gets u = πn, zz = πn²/4 and retardation 4λp/n, which matches the square of side n. The next page's n = z/√π is also the radius relation, so the slip is verbal: 'diametrum' should read 'semidiametrum/radius'. The final expression 2λp√π/z is correct either way.

Physical rather than mathematical: making friction proportional to wall pressure (a Coulomb dry-friction analogy) is wrong for real pipe flow. There, wall shear is essentially independent of static pressure and depends on velocity, as in the Chézy, Darcy-Weisbach and Hagen-Poiseuille laws. Euler's λ is therefore not a meaningful material constant.

ideas.what: Wall friction on a fluid slice taken proportional to the normal pressure on the wetted wall (Coulomb/Amontons law transferred to fluids)
ideas.modern_name: pressure-proportional (Coulomb-type) wall friction model; superseded by velocity-dependent wall shear stress
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (E260) is the usual reference for this specific (incorrect) hypothesis
ideas.where_published: E260, Novi Comm. Acad. Petrop. 6 (1761); discussed in histories of hydraulics (unsure of exact commentary locations)

ideas.what: Friction retardation per unit mass proportional to wetted perimeter / cross-sectional area, so shape enters only through u/A
ideas.modern_name: hydraulic radius (hydraulic mean depth) R = A/P
ideas.usually_credited_to: Chézy (1775) and Du Buat (1779) in open-channel and pipe hydraulics
ideas.where_published: E260 (this page); unsure whether earlier hydraulic writers already used perimeter/area

ideas.what: Comparison of rectangular, square and circular sections, and absorbing π into an empirical coefficient α
ideas.modern_name: shape dependence through hydraulic radius; empirical friction coefficient

missed.claim: Euler's 1761 retardation ∝ (wetted perimeter)/(area) is an explicit use of the hydraulic-radius ratio more than a decade before Chézy (1775) and Du Buat (1779). The hydraulic radius is not usually attributed to Euler. His underlying friction law differs (pressure- rather than velocity-dependent), but the geometric reduction to P/A is identical. This is a modest priority note for the history of the hydraulic radius, perhaps already remarked by historians of hydraulics (unsure).
missed.quote: Pendet ergo frictio tam a quantitate, quam a figura cauitatis tubi ... erit perimeter eius u=2m+2n, et area zz=mn
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: It is a historical-priority point for the hydraulic radius concept; there is no mathematical novelty.

deep.surprise_reason: The perimeter/area (hydraulic radius) dependence appearing in Euler before Chézy and Du Buat is a mildly interesting priority detail. E260 itself is known, and its friction law is physically wrong and superseded.
transcription_corrections: Sec. 9: the transcription has 'λ esse fractionem valde paruam'. The scan is ambiguous between 'fractio-nem' and 'frictio-nem'; 'fractionem' (a very small fraction) is grammatically and mathematically the sensible reading.
The transcription is otherwise faithful. Note that the printed text itself says 'diametrum' where the formulas imply the radius (see errors).
